title: The great banquet (Luke 14:15–24)
hookLine: the invited guests make excuses, so the host fills the hall with the poor and the lame

cards: Jesus is at dinner in the house of a leading Pharisee, and a guest says, happily, how blessed will be the one who eats bread in the kingdom of God. Jesus answers with a dinner story.
A man plans a great supper, invites many people, and they all say yes. When the food is ready, his servant goes out: come, it's ready. And one by one, they make excuses.
I just bought a field, I have to go and see it. I just bought five pairs of oxen, I have to try them out. I just got married, so I can't come.
The hall is set, the food is hot, and every chair is empty.

teach.b: Some readers think the first listeners laughed out loud at those excuses. Who buys a field without seeing it, or ten oxen without testing them? These aren't reasons.
They're ways of saying: I have better things to do.
These guests had been invited ahead, said yes, and been called again when the meal was ready. Every one backed out at the last minute. The host is angry.
He tells his servant: "Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind." People never invited anywhere.
The servant comes back: there's still room.
So the host sends him further, past the town to the roads and the hedges, where travelers and people with nowhere to go are, and says: "compel them to come in, that my house may be filled."
Compel sounds harsh, but think who's being asked.

teach.h: THAT MY HOUSE MAY BE FILLED.
teach.b: Someone sleeping by a hedge, told a rich man wants him at dinner, might say: that can't be for me. He'd have to be talked into it.
A few verses earlier, Jesus tells his own host the same thing: when you give a feast, invite the poor, the maimed, the lame and the blind, the people who can't invite you back.

Christians often read the banquet as a picture of the kingdom of God: a table that stays set, where the empty chairs fill with people nobody expected. It's also about the ones asked first, who chose their fields instead.

how: Churches often run community meals, food pantries and open tables where anyone can eat, and some Christians make a point of inviting people who are usually left out.

o: to force someone in against their will
to urge hard, not taking no for an answer
to welcome someone politely at the door

games.q: who said or did what — tap the pairs.
p: the poor, the maimed, the halt, the blind

s: the guests had never been invited
they'd been invited and said yes. they backed out when the meal was ready.
Jesus told this story at a Pharisee's dinner table
Luke sets it in the house of a leading Pharisee, over a sabbath meal.
the host stops once the hall is half full
the servant says there's still room, and he's sent out again, to the roads and the hedges.

games.q: you're the host. the food is hot, and every guest has sent an excuse. what do you do?
o: send out for the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind.
games.why: he fills the hall with the people nobody invites, then sends out again, because there's still room.

practice: Let a few faces come up of people rarely invited: the new person at work who eats alone, the friend who hears about the party afterward. Let one face stay, and picture them at your table, over a coffee or in a saved seat.

wordCard.voice: Compel. The host's word to his servant, sent out to bring in the people who'd never believe a feast like this could be for them.

orig.note: Greek: supper, the main meal of the day. Luke's host makes a "great" one.

carryVoice: Your line: there's room at the table. The empty chairs were never meant to stay empty. Pull up a chair.

sources.q: Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind.
compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
